title: Exposure to the Chinese famine in early life and the risk of anaemia in adulthood.
ehr_evidence: We used the data of 2007 adults born between 1954 and 1964 in Jiangsu province from the 2002 Chinese National Nutrition and Health Survey (data collected via in-person interviews, anthropometric measurements, fasting blood samples, and 3-day weighed food diaries, not an EHR/claims/registry).
summary: A cross-sectional study of 2007 adults born 1954-1964 in Jiangsu province, China, examining whether fetal early-life exposure to the 1959-1961 Chinese famine is associated with increased risk of anaemia in adulthood.
key_findings: Fetal exposure to famine was associated with a 37% increased risk of adult anaemia versus non-exposed after adjustment (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.09-1.71).
The association was stronger among men (RR 1.87, 95% CI 1.21-2.87) than women (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.90-1.53), though the interaction was not statistically significant.
The association was strongest among overweight/obese individuals (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.20-2.56) and those with low education (RR 2.07, 95% CI 1.37-3.12).
There was no significant association between famine exposure and anaemia among urban residents, with a significant interaction between residence (urban/rural) and famine exposure (p=0.023).
Haemoglobin levels were lower in the fetal-exposed cohort (regression coefficients -0.32 in men, -0.24 in men and women combined).
captured_features: anaemia status (Hb <13 g/dl men, <12 g/dl women)
famine exposure cohort (non-exposed, fetal, early/mid/late childhood)
population: 2007 adults (905 men, 1102 women) born 1954-1964 in Jiangsu province, China, aged ~38-49 in 2002
limitations: No information on iron metabolism biomarkers or menstruation status in women that may affect body iron stores and anaemia.
Regional differences in famine severity were not assessed due to small numbers in the fetal-exposed group.
Selection bias possible due to selective mortality and reduced fertility across famine exposure groups.
Small sample size in some subgroups limited power of stratified analyses, making findings suggestive rather than conclusive.
